newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Ministers hint at breaking EMU pact deadlock.
newsitem.headline: Ministers hint at breaking EMU pact deadlock.

text.p: European Union finance ministers showed signs of progress on Monday towards breaking a deadlock on a new system for ensuring that states in a single currency, planned for 1999, maintain budgetary discipline after joining.

Negotiations on a budget stability pact have been stalled over German demands for stringent rules -- triggering protests that Germany is trying to impose its own tough monetary policies on the rest of the EU.
German Finance Minister Theo Waigel was expected to arrive at Monday's gathering later in the afternoon, and ministers said talks on the issue would wait until then.

But Juergen Stark, German state secretary for finance, told a news conference there could be agreement on the broad parameters of the pact when EU leaders meet in a summit in Dublin on December 13 and 14.
"There will be political agreement over the main elements. I see that achievable," Stark told journalists. "What we will not have accomplished is the final negotiation on the legal text."

German Chancellor Helmut Kohl said after meeting French President Jacques Chirac at the weekend that he did not wish to interfere in France's domestic policies but that the two countries agreed on the need for currency stability.
Taking a slightly cautious stance at the Brussells talks, Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer, Kenneth Clarke, said it is was still unclear how much progress there would be on the budget accord.
"It's too soon to say whether we will reach agreement," he told a news conference.
The effort to secure a budget stability pact has become one of the most difficult hurdles in nailing down a blueprint for economic and monetary union (EMU).
Under a proposed plan, countries running annual deficits above three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) could face stiff fines if they failed to curb expenditure.
But if a government could show that a severe recession was behind the deterioration of its public finances, it might be able to avoid sanctions.

Germany wants a recession defined as a two percent annual decline in GDP. Others have argued for a less rigid approach, preferring a range -- a fall in output of between 0.5 and 2.0 percent. That would force EU finance ministers to decide whether fines were appropriate.
French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said the decision on whether a government had an excessive deficit should be made after a proper evaluation of a country's economic circumstances.
"France's position is simple and clear. It is up to the (finance ministers) to decide on a case by case basis," Arthuis said in a newspaper interview published on Monday.
Taking a shot at Germany's tough bargaining stance, Arthuis added: "When you're in a community you have to try to reach a consensus rather than imposing your point of view."

Britain's Clarke, facing an upsurge of anti-European sentiment in his ruling Conservative party at home, said he would make sure that the British government would reserve judgement on any political decision taken on Monday.

On negotiations over the legal framework for monetary union, Clarke said he secured a change in proposed legislation that would not bind any countries not participating in the common currency in 1999.

Separately, the ministers are likely to agree a blueprint for a new Exchange Rate Mechanism that will link the single currency to those of EU nations not participating among the first wave of countries in 1999.
